Abstract

We predict the redshift of galaxies, a measure of their distance, from their brightness in the five SDSS filters. The data are 100 galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (DR18) with spectroscopic redshifts between 0.025 and 0.221. They were cleaned with AI assistance and split into 80 training and 20 test galaxies. Four supervised models (linear regression, k-nearest neighbours, random forest and support vector regression) were tuned by repeated cross-validation in R and compared with a mean-prediction baseline. In cross-validation the best model was M4 SVR (RMSE 0.0208 vs 0.0419 for the baseline). On the held-out test set the best model was M3 Random Forest (RMSE 0.0331, σNMAD 0.0285, no catastrophic outliers). The colour g − r is by far the most important predictor, and predicted redshift rises steadily with it. This is the signature of the 4000 Å break moving through the g filter as galaxies recede.

1 Introduction and physics background

1.1 Redshift

Light from a receding galaxy is stretched to longer wavelengths:

\[ z = \frac{\lambda_{\text{obs}} - \lambda_{\text{emit}}}{\lambda_{\text{emit}}}, \qquad \lambda_{\text{obs}} = (1+z)\,\lambda_{\text{emit}}. \]

At low redshift, Hubble’s law gives \(v \approx cz = H_0 d\), so the redshift measures distance.

1.2 Spectroscopic versus photometric redshift

A spectroscopic redshift comes from the shift of spectral lines. It is very precise but slow and expensive to obtain. A photometric redshift estimates z from the brightness in a few broad filters. It is less precise but works for billions of galaxies, which is essential for surveys such as LSST, Euclid and DES. Galaxies that have both measurements let us learn the mapping from photometry to redshift: a supervised regression problem.

1.3 Why colours encode redshift: the 4000 Å break

Older stellar populations produce a sharp drop in galaxy spectra blueward of 4000 Å. As z increases, the break appears at \(4000(1+z)\) Å and removes flux from the bluer filter, so the colour (magnitude difference) between filters changes. Figure F20 shows that, for the redshift range of this sample, the break always lies inside the g band. We therefore expect g − r to redden with redshift and to be the most informative feature. The r magnitude adds distance information because, in a flux-limited sample, more distant galaxies look fainter (inverse-square law).

Figure F20. Observed wavelength of the 4000 Å break, 4000(1 + z) Å (black line), over the SDSS filter bands (shaded: effective wavelength ± FWHM/2, approximate). The grey band marks this sample (z = 0.025–0.221), where the break lies at 4098–4885 Å, inside the g band. It would leave g only at z ≈ 0.34.

1.4 Aim and hypotheses

Can a galaxy’s colours predict its redshift? We test four hypotheses:

  • H1: g − r is the most important predictor.
  • H2: predicted redshift rises monotonically with g − r.
  • H3: non-linear models (k-NN, random forest, SVR) beat linear regression.
  • H4: all models beat the mean-prediction baseline.

2 Data

2.1 Acquisition

120 random galaxies were retrieved from SDSS DR18 with a SkyServer SQL query (data/sql/sdss_query.sql) by R/01_acquire.R. The query keeps spectroscopically confirmed galaxies with reliable redshifts (zWarning = 0), clean photometry, the Main Galaxy Sample flux limit 14 ≤ r ≤ 17.77, 0.01 < z < 0.5 and magnitude errors below 0.2. Magnitudes are corrected for Milky Way dust (dered_*). The raw file is frozen and recorded with an MD5 checksum in data/raw/ACQUISITION.md.

2.2 AI-assisted inspection and cleaning

Following workflow step 2, an AI assistant (Claude Code) inspected the raw data’s structure, missing and sentinel values, duplicates, ranges and colour outliers, then proposed cleaning rules. The student reviewed every rule. Each rule logs its row counts (Table T02), and every AI interaction is recorded in the appendix. The data contained no missing values, sentinels or duplicates. The colour-outlier rule (median ± 5·MAD) removed 2 galaxies that were blue in all colours. The AI suggested keeping them as probably real star-forming galaxies; the student chose to apply the planned rule. A random sample of 100 galaxies (seed 42) forms the analysis set.

Table T02. Cleaning log: each rule and the rows it removed.

2.4 Exploratory physics

Figure F03. u − g versus g − r for the 100 galaxies, coloured by spectroscopic redshift. Higher-redshift galaxies sit at redder g − r.

Figure F04. Colours of 100 SDSS galaxies versus spectroscopic redshift. Solid lines are LOESS fits with 95% bands; r is the Pearson correlation. g − r has the strongest correlation (r = 0.54): it reddens as the 4000 Å break moves through the g band.

Figure F05. Pearson correlations among the five features and z_spec. The feature most correlated with redshift is g − r (r = 0.54).

3 Methods

3.1 Features and target

The target is the spectroscopic redshift. The features are the four colours u − g, g − r, r − i, i − z and the r-band magnitude. Colours remove the overall brightness and keep the shape of the spectrum, while r carries the brightness–distance information.

3.2 Train/test split

A stratified split on redshift (caret::createDataPartition, seed 42) gives 80 training and 20 test galaxies. A two-sample KS test finds no difference between their redshift distributions (D = 0.088, p = 0.999, Figure F07). The test set was not used for any training, tuning or preprocessing decision.

Figure F07. Spectroscopic redshift of the 80 training and 20 test galaxies (histograms, kernel densities and rugs) after a stratified 80/20 split (seed 42). Two-sample KS test: D = 0.088, p = 0.999, so there is no evidence that the two distributions differ.

3.3 Models and tuning

All models use redshift ~ u_g + g_r + r_i + i_z + r and the same 25 resamples (5-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times) on the training set. Hyperparameters were chosen by the lowest mean CV RMSE (Table T03). Centring and scaling were fitted inside each training fold.

Table T03. Hyperparameter grids and selected values.
Model Parameter Search grid Selected
M0 Baseline (none) predicts the training mean —
M1 Linear (none) ordinary least squares —
M2 k-NN k 1, 2, …, 20 8
M3 Random Forest mtry 1, 2, …, 5 5
M3 Random Forest ntree fixed 500
M4 SVR C 2^-2, 2^-1, …, 2^6 32
M4 SVR sigma 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1 0.01

3.4 Metrics

With \(\Delta z = (z_{\text{phot}} - z_{\text{spec}})/(1 + z_{\text{spec}})\) we report RMSE, MAE, \(R^2 = 1 - SS_{\text{res}}/SS_{\text{tot}}\), bias = mean(Δz), the robust scatter \(\sigma_{\text{NMAD}} = 1.4826 \times \text{median}(|\Delta z - \text{median}(\Delta z)|)\) and the catastrophic-outlier fraction η = fraction with |Δz| > 0.15. Test metrics carry 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (2000 resamples).

5 Discussion: physics interpretation

5.1 Which features matter and why

Table T06. Feature importance: random-forest permutation importance and standardised linear-regression coefficients with 95% CIs.
Feature RF %IncMSE RF rank LM std. coef. LM CI low LM CI high LM rank
g − r 44.2704 1 0.0611 0.0504 0.0719 1
u − g 13.6076 2 -0.0352 -0.0438 -0.0266 2
r (mag) 8.9287 3 0.0085 0.0031 0.0139 4
i − z 7.5409 4 -0.0095 -0.0170 -0.0019 3
r − i 4.7368 5 -0.0076 -0.0163 0.0011 5

Figure F18. Feature importance. Left: random-forest permutation importance (%IncMSE). Right: standardised linear-regression coefficients with 95% CIs (change in predicted z per 1 SD of each feature). Most important: g − r (RF) and g − r (LM).

Figure F19. Partial dependence of the random-forest redshift prediction on g − r and r − i (training data; rugs show the observed values). Over the observed range, predicted z changes by 0.099 with g − r (Spearman ρ = 0.98).

The random forest ranks g − r first (%IncMSE 44.27), and the partial dependence (Figure F19) shows predicted redshift climbing steadily with g − r. This is the behaviour expected from the 4000 Å break moving redward through the g filter: the galaxy loses flux in g relative to r and its g − r colour reddens. r − i correlates with z on its own (Figure F04) but adds little once g − r is known, because the two colours are strongly correlated (Figure F05).

  • Random-forest ranking: 1. g − r (%IncMSE 44.3); 2. u − g (%IncMSE 13.6); 3. r (mag) (%IncMSE 8.9); 4. i − z (%IncMSE 7.5); 5. r − i (%IncMSE 4.7).
  • Most important feature: g − r (random forest), g − r (largest |standardised coefficient| in the linear model).
  • r magnitude: RF rank 3 of 5; LM coefficient 0.0085 [95% CI 0.0031, 0.0139]: positive, so fainter galaxies are predicted at higher z, as the inverse-square law expects.
  • u − g: almost no correlation with z on its own (training r = -0.02) but RF rank 2 and LM coefficient -0.0352 [-0.0438, -0.0266] at fixed g − r. Interpretation: u − g traces galaxy type (old/red vs star-forming/blue), which lets the models tell an intrinsically red galaxy from one reddened by redshift in g − r.
  • The colours are strongly correlated with each other (F05), so individual linear coefficients can trade off against each other; their CIs are wide.

5.2 Hypotheses

  • H1 (g − r is the most important predictor): supported by both RF and LM.
  • H2 (predicted z rises monotonically with g − r): supported. Spearman ρ of the RF partial-dependence curve = 0.98 (threshold 0.8).
  • H3 (non-linear models beat linear regression): CV partly supported (only M4 SVR beat LM); test partly supported (only M3 Random Forest, M4 SVR beat LM). CV RMSE: LM 0.0226, k-NN 0.0324, RF 0.0305, SVR 0.0208. Test RMSE: LM 0.0410, k-NN 0.0428, RF 0.0331, SVR 0.0391.
  • H4 (all models beat the mean baseline): CV supported, test supported (point estimates; baseline CV 0.0419, test 0.0457). The test CIs in T05 overlap the baseline for 3 of 4 learners.

5.3 Where the models fail

Cross-validation ranks M4 SVR first, but on the test set M3 Random Forest is best. The difference comes from a few test galaxies whose colours lie outside the range seen in training (4 of 20). One of them has a red u − g but unusually blue g − r, r − i and i − z. The linear model and the near-linear SVR extrapolate for it and predict a negative, unphysical redshift (2 predictions below zero in total). A random forest predicts averages of training redshifts and cannot leave the training range, so it is more robust to such galaxies. Every model also pulls the lowest- and highest-redshift galaxies towards the mean redshift (Figure F15), a typical effect of a small training set.

With only 20 test galaxies the confidence intervals in Table T05 overlap strongly, so no model is clearly better than another on this test set. The robust scatter σNMAD of 0.0285 (95% CI 0.0123–0.0435) falls within the ≈ 0.02–0.03 reported for SDSS photo-z trained on hundreds of thousands of galaxies. With only 80 training galaxies and a narrow redshift range this is encouraging, but the wide interval means the comparison is not precise. The learning curves (Figure F12) show the gap between training and test error for each model as the training set grows.

  • Test galaxies with at least one feature outside the training range: 4 of 20.
  • Negative (unphysical) test predictions: 2 (M1 Linear, M4 SVR). Linear and kernel models can extrapolate beyond the training redshifts; random-forest predictions are averages of training redshifts and cannot.
  • Over this sample’s redshift range (0.025–0.221) the 4000 Å break stays inside the g band (F20), so the redshift signal is the break moving within g, which reddens g − r.

6 Limitations

  • Small sample. n = 100 is set by the assignment brief. Real photo-z work uses 105–106 training galaxies.
  • Small test set. With 20 galaxies, metrics have wide confidence intervals and η can only change in steps of 5%.
  • Narrow redshift range. The models are valid only for 0.025 ≤ z ≤ 0.221 and r ≤ 17.77. In this range the break never leaves the g band.
  • Very blue galaxies excluded. The 5·MAD cleaning rule removed galaxies that are blue in every colour, so the models have not learned such objects.
  • Unphysical extrapolation. The linear model and SVR can predict z < 0 for galaxies with colours outside the training range.
  • Unused information. Magnitude errors were not used as weights or inputs.

7 Conclusion

Five-band SDSS photometry predicts galaxy redshift better than a mean-value baseline, even with only 80 training galaxies. On the test set the best model, M3 Random Forest, reaches RMSE 0.0331 against 0.0457 for the baseline. Every learner beats the baseline on the point estimate, but only M3 Random Forest has a 95% confidence interval entirely below it, so with 20 test galaxies the improvement is clear only for that model. The models learn the physics: g − r, which tracks the 4000 Å break moving through the g filter, dominates the predictions, and predicted redshift rises monotonically with it. Smooth models (linear regression, SVR) do best in cross-validation, while the random forest is the most robust on unusual test galaxies because it cannot extrapolate to unphysical values.

Centring and scaling are not done here. They run inside caret::train() on each training fold, so the test set cannot leak into them.

8.0.0.2.8 AI-008 — Model training and tuning
  • Date: 2026-10-18
  • Stage: Modelling (code)
  • Tool / model: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5)
  • Input given to AI: train.csv (via the script). test.csv is used only to score the learning-curve refits after tuning.
  • Prompt (short): “Write and run R/05_train.R (baseline, LM, kNN, RF, SVR with shared repeated-CV folds, T03, T04, F08–F13).”
  • AI output / suggestion:
    • One fixed set of 25 resamples (createMultiFolds, 5-fold × 5, seed 42) is passed to every model through trainControl(index = ...), so all models are compared on identical folds.
    • The baseline uses caret’s built-in "null" model (predicts the training mean), so it goes through the same folds as the learners.
    • A custom summaryFunction scores CV with the same RMSE, MAE and R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot definitions as the test evaluation. caret’s default R² is the squared correlation, which is undefined for the constant baseline.
    • Grids exactly as in D-008/D-010. XGBoost (optional M5) was not added.
    • Learning curves: 7 sizes × 20 repeats × 5 models = 700 refits with frozen hyperparameters (D-016).
    • Checked every figure visually. The F11 labels were unreadable on dark cells, so they now switch to white.
    • Re-running gives identical T03, T04 and learning-curve tables. Runtime is about 40 s.
  • Observations for the report (no modelling choice was changed):
    • SVR’s best σ = 0.01 is the smallest value in the grid (a smooth, nearly linear kernel), and RF’s best mtry = 5 uses all features. Both sit at the edge of their grids.
    • In the learning curves (F12), test-set RMSE at n = 80 is clearly higher than CV RMSE for the linear and SVR models. Phase 7’s residual plots should show whether one or two test galaxies cause this.
  • Owner decision: Accepted. The owner committed it.
  • Resulting code: R/05_train.R; randomForest and kernlab added to renv.lock
  • Effect on data: none (models saved to outputs/models/, git-ignored)
  • Linked decision: D-008, D-010, D-014, D-016
8.0.0.2.9 AI-009 — Test-set evaluation
  • Date: 2026-10-18
  • Stage: Evaluation (code)
  • Tool / model: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5)
  • Input given to AI: the saved models and test.csv (via the script).
  • Prompt (short): “Write and run R/06_evaluate.R (test metrics with bootstrap CIs, T05, test_predictions.csv, F14–F17).”
  • AI output / suggestion:
    • Wrote R/06_evaluate.R. It predicts with the saved models unchanged, computes RMSE, MAE, R², bias, σ_NMAD and η (utils_metrics.R) and 95% percentile bootstrap CIs (2000 resamples, seed 42) for RMSE, R² and σ_NMAD. It writes T05 and test_predictions.csv and draws F14–F17. A re-run gives byte-identical tables.
    • Checked every figure visually and fixed label overlaps in F14 and F17.
    • Diagnosed why test RMSE is higher than CV RMSE for the linear model and SVR, using the largest-|Δz| list the script prints and a one-off check of feature ranges (not part of the pipeline). One test galaxy (1237661950779588703) has a red u − g but g − r, r − i and i − z at the blue edge of the training set, with r − i below the training minimum. The linear model and the near-linear SVR extrapolate and predict a negative redshift for it. Random-forest predictions are averages of training redshifts, so they cannot leave the training range, which is why RF has the lowest test RMSE. In total, 4 of the 20 test galaxies have at least one colour outside the training range.
    • All learners predict the lowest-z test galaxy too high: no training galaxy is that close, so predictions are pulled towards the mean (F15).
  • Owner decision: Accepted. The owner committed it. No modelling choice was changed after seeing the test results (AGENTS.md R5).
  • Notes for the report: the 95% CIs overlap heavily, so with only 20 test galaxies no model is clearly better than another. The CV ranking (SVR ≈ LM > RF > k-NN) differs from the test ranking (RF best). Report both and explain the extrapolation effect. Negative z_phot is unphysical, and that belongs in Limitations.
  • Resulting code: R/06_evaluate.R
  • Effect on data: none (read-only)
  • Linked decision: D-011, D-014
8.0.0.2.10 AI-010 — Physics interpretation
  • Date: 2026-10-18
  • Stage: Interpretation (code)
  • Tool / model: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5)
  • Input given to AI: the saved LM and RF models, the train/test CSVs and T04, T05 and test_predictions.csv (via the script).
  • Prompt (short): “Write and run R/07_interpret.R (T06 feature importance, F18, F19 partial dependence, interpretation_notes.md).”
  • AI output / suggestion:
    • T06 combines RF permutation importance (%IncMSE) with standardised LM coefficients, their 95% CIs and p-values, and ranks each. F18 shows both side by side, built with patchwork. F19 shows the RF partial dependence on g − r and r − i (pdp, training data only).
    • interpretation_notes.md turns H1–H4 into verdicts computed from the tables, so the report does not depend on typed-in numbers. H3 has three outcomes (supported, partly supported, not supported) and names the models, rather than a single yes or no.
    • Added an interpretation line about u − g. It barely correlates with z on its own but is the second most important feature, with a negative coefficient at fixed g − r. The AI’s explanation: u − g traces galaxy type, which separates intrinsic redness from redshift reddening in g − r. This is a physical interpretation for the owner to check, not a tested result.
    • Checked F18 and F19 visually. The script runs without warnings, and a re-run gives byte-identical T06 and notes.
  • Owner decision: Accepted. The owner committed it.
  • Resulting code: R/07_interpret.R; pdp and patchwork added to renv.lock
  • Effect on data: none (read-only)
  • Linked decision: D-006, D-008
